outcome: No progress on the infinitude question was found; only new individual terms of the underlying sequence were discovered by distributed computing, which does not narrow the existence question.
summary: A Kummer prime, as Wikipedia's list uses the term, is a prime of the form p_n# − 1 (a primorial minus one; OEIS A057704 lists the indices n for which this is prime). The question 'are there infinitely many?' is a pure existence question and remains completely open: no proof, disproof, heuristic breakthrough, or expert commentary addressing the infinitude of this sequence was found anywhere. What did happen since 26 January 2024 is that PrimeGrid's distributed sieving project found three new terms of the sequence: n = 334023, 435582, and 446895, credited to Jeppe Stig Nielsen and reported on OEIS A057704 (added 16 Dec 2024), with the largest (6533299# − 1, 2,835,864 digits) also documented on Wikipedia's Primorial prime article (dated to August 2024 by a search-engine synthesis citing Christian Wallbaum/PrimeGrid; the Wikipedia article itself gives a vaguer 'as of July 2025' framing, likely reflecting when the article prose was last edited rather than the discovery date). Per §3.1, a new record term of a sequence like this is not a narrowing of an existence question — it says nothing about whether the sequence is infinite, so it does not count as progress on this bullet. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this area: the new terms were found using conventional distributed sieving and primality-proving software (PrimeGrid's standard toolchain, e.g. MultiSieve/mtsieve and PRP/proof software), not any machine-learning or LLM system. Searches for any AI system engaging with Kummer primes specifically, or with the closely related (but distinct) conjecture on infinitely many regular primes, turned up nothing tying an AI system to either question. I am confident nothing was missed: the topic is a narrow, well-tracked computational sequence with an actively maintained OEIS entry and a Wikipedia article, both checked directly, and general web searches for AI-related activity on the term also came up empty.
competing_reading: One could argue that the ongoing PrimeGrid discovery campaign constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense (extending computational search), similar to how a bound moving counts as progress in other problems. But §3.1 explicitly excludes this: 'a search verified to a larger limit' is not progress on an infinitude question unless the record itself is the object of the question, which it is not here (the bullet asks about existence of infinitely many, not about the current largest known example).
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude for primes of form p_n# − 1, or a heuristic/asymptotic result specifically bearing on whether the sequence is finite or infinite (analogous to results on Mersenne or Fermat primes) — none of which currently exists.
